brief.headline: Asia-Mediterranean container rates jump $1,076 per FEU to $5,357 while Asia-US lanes ease, raising costs for Morocco, Spain and France-bound cargo.
brief.overview: Asia-Mediterranean container rates rose $1,076 to $5,357 per FEU in week 47, which will lift quotes for Morocco, Spain and France-bound cargo, while Asia-US lanes fell. Morocco is preparing a national fleet plan of 21 new vessels by 2030 and Atlantic port traffic is gaining weight, although near-term operations are unlikely to change. In Spain, international ro-ro short-sea volumes slipped 1% in 2025, with Atlantic traffic down 8.7%. Rhine water levels at Kaub rebounded, cutting barge freight from Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp to Basel from €162.5 to €92.5 per tonne.

highlights.text: Asia-Mediterranean container rates jump $1,076 to $5,357 per FEU, raising costs for Morocco, Spain and France.

Morocco plans a 21-ship national merchant fleet by 2030 that could shift some Europe-Morocco volumes to local operators.
Spanish international ro-ro volumes fell 1% in 2025, with Atlantic traffic down 8.7% while Mediterranean links grew.
EU and Indonesia signed a CEPA removing duties on more than 98% of EU exports, but it takes effect only in early 2027.
Zim's third-quarter net income rose to $830 million as freight rates climbed 55%, keeping costs high on transpacific lanes.

brief.market: Asia-Mediterranean container rates rose sharply while Asia-US West Coast and East Coast rates fell, and Zim expects costs to stay high on Asia-US lanes. Vehicle carrier charter rates near $100,000 per day and rising vessel values point to a capacity crunch, while tanker freight has weakened as refining margins fall. Intra-Asia rates were mixed, with Shanghai to Jebel Ali remaining high at $8,149 per 40ft container.

items.title: Sovcomflot credits sanctions adaptation for profit rebound as EU targets its former fleet network
items.originalTitle: Sovcomflot credits sanctions adaptation for profit rebound as EU targets network behind former fleet
items.summary: Russian shipping company Sovcomflot has attributed a return to profit to its adaptation to sanctions. At the same time, the EU is targeting the network of companies behind vessels that were formerly part of the Sovcomflot fleet.
items.impact: Sanctions on Sovcomflot and linked shipping networks raise compliance risk for forwarders and agents handling cargo on tonnage with Russian ownership or links. Vessels moved between owners or flags may still fall within EU measures, so counterparties need careful screening. The source is only a short summary, so the specific measures and dates are not confirmed here.
items.action: Screen vessels, owners and managers on any voyage touching Russian-linked tonnage against current EU sanctions lists, and watch for the detailed EU listings and their effective dates.

items.title: Rhine water levels rebound at Kaub, easing barge freight costs and shortages
items.originalTitle: Water levels on Rhine rise, providing relief to market participants
items.summary: Water levels on the Rhine rose above 140 cm at Kaub on 20 November and were forecast to exceed 250 cm by 22 November after several days of rain. Barge freight from the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub to Basel fell from €162.5/mt to €92.5/mt over the same week, after months of record lows that had constrained cargo loads.
items.impact: Barges carrying more than 2,000 tonnes must cut loads below 150 cm, and shipowners have been adding surcharges to offset lost capacity, so cost relief will depend on sustained levels. Stocks remain very low and a backlog still needs clearing, while planned refinery turnarounds and Rhine lock maintenance in the first quarter could tighten supply and logistics again.
items.action: Watch Kaub gauge readings and barge surcharge notices over the coming weeks, and plan for possible Q1 constraints from refinery turnarounds and lock maintenance. Use rail where available, as the right-bank Middle Rhine Line rail route reopens on 12 December.

items.title: Asia-Mediterranean container rates jump $1,076 while Asia-US lanes fall in week 47
items.originalTitle: Container Report – Week 47
items.summary: The Baltic Exchange Freightos-style FBX Weighted Average fell 57 points to 3,419 over the past week, with mixed movement across lanes. Asia-US West Coast (FBX01) dropped $809 to $7,643/FEU and Asia-US East Coast (FBX03) fell $427 to $9,421/FEU, while Asia-North Europe (FBX11) edged up to $3,406/FEU. The largest rise was on Asia-Mediterranean (FBX13), up $1,076 to $5,357/FEU, and North Europe-US East Coast (FBX22) softened $107 to $2,639/FEU.
items.impact: The sharp rise on Asia-Mediterranean lanes will raise costs for Morocco, Spain, France and Italian-bound cargo, so forwarders should expect higher quotes on that trade. Falling Asia-US rates may ease transpacific costs, but the report flags a possible strike at Los Angeles and Long Beach this weekend, which could cause delays and make rate direction uncertain. Rates on Asia-North Europe remain much lower than Asia-Mediterranean.
items.action: Check current quotations on Asia-Mediterranean and confirm surcharges with carriers before committing to shipments. Monitor news on the possible Los Angeles and Long Beach strike and build contingency time into US West Coast bookings.

items.title: Zim's third-quarter profit surges to $830 million as freight rates rise 55%
items.originalTitle: Zim Q3 profit surges to $830 million as freight rates jump 55%
items.summary: Israeli carrier Zim reported third-quarter net income of $830 million, up from $123 million a year earlier, as average freight rates climbed 55% to $2,480 per TEU. It raised its full-year adjusted EBITDA and EBIT guidance, and said the proposed Hapag-Lloyd takeover is targeted to close in the first quarter of 2027. Reported profit includes a non-cash impairment reversal of $155 million after tax.
items.impact: Strong pricing on Asia-US West Coast and East Coast lanes signals tight capacity and elevated rates, so forwarders should expect costs to stay high. Management said it saw some softening in recent weeks around the year-end holidays, with a possible pick-up in January before Chinese New Year. Zim also launched ZX3 and Falcon services, adding expedited options for Asia-US West Coast and China to South America cargo.
items.action: Review contract and spot rate exposure on Asia-US lanes and monitor rates for the expected January recovery. Consider the new expedited Asia-US West Coast and China-South America services where faster transit matters.

items.title: Vehicle carrier charter rates near $100,000 per day as vessel values climb
items.originalTitle: Vehicle carrier charter rates near $100,000 per day while vessel values climb amid capacity crunch
items.summary: Vehicle carrier charter rates are reported near $100,000 per day while vessel values are rising amid a capacity crunch. The source attributes rising demand to changing trade patterns, longer-haul trades and Cape of Good Hope diversions. The short summary notes that record newbuild contracting is under way across the industry.
items.impact: Higher charter costs and tight vehicle carrier capacity may raise rates and reduce space availability for car and rolling cargo shipments. Longer routings via the Cape of Good Hope can extend transit times, so schedules for vehicle and roll-on cargo may need more buffer. Rising vessel values suggest owners expect sustained demand rather than a short-lived spike.
items.action: Check current vehicle carrier space and rate quotes with carriers and monitor charter and newbuild trends for signs of easing as new tonnage enters service.

items.title: Lower refining margins squeeze tanker freight rates across clean and crude markets
items.originalTitle: Tanker Market: Lower Refining Margins Leaving Less Room to Pay for Freight
items.summary: Gibson reports that weaker refining margins are leaving refiners less room to pay freight, so cost pressure is shifting to sellers and freight has already fallen. Clean tanker rates outside the Gulf have dropped sharply, with US Gulf MRs around $26,000/day and TC15 LR2s at $60,000/day against $175,000/day in mid-October. Chinese clean product export plans for the final two months of quota may not be met in full.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers buying tanker capacity may see lower clean and crude freight rates in the near term, but rates could recover if margins stay weak only to a limited extent. Fleet supply is growing, with scheduled deliveries through 2027, while attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have temporarily removed some capacity. Risk premiums remain high in Gulf freight, where war risk sets the price.
items.action: Monitor weekly clean and dirty tanker rates, Chinese export quota use in the coming months, and whether Gulf refinery runs show up in product loadings. Consider timing tanker bookings against the current softening in clean rates, while allowing for Hormuz security risk.

items.title: Drewry intra-Asia index edges up $4 to $1,444 per 40ft container
items.originalTitle: Drewry: Intra Asia Container Index Keeps Grinding Higher
items.summary: Drewry's Intra-Asia Container Index rose $4 to $1,444 per 40ft container, with rates broadly stable. Easing congestion on the Greater China to North Asia corridor, notably to Busan, offset rising rates to Southeast Asia, Manila and Singapore. Drewry expects rates to decline in the coming weeks as extra capacity and better port conditions ease pressure.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers buying intra-Asia capacity face mixed movements by lane, so spot quotes should be checked route by route rather than against the composite index. Shanghai to Jebel Ali remains high at $8,149 per 40ft container, and congestion at Singapore is adding waiting time at a key transhipment hub. Weather-related port closures and vessel delays could still push rates up, and elevated bunker costs continue to support pricing.
items.action: Watch weekly index updates and Singapore waiting times before fixing intra-Asia spot bookings, and monitor the OOCL FCS4 service linking Chennai and Visakhapatnam with Port Klang when it launches.

items.title: Morocco plans 21-ship national merchant fleet by 2030 to cut reliance on foreign carriers
items.originalTitle: Flotte maritime: le Maroc prépare son grand retour en mer
items.summary: Morocco is preparing to rebuild a national merchant fleet, with a roadmap drawn up by Boston Consulting Group for the Ministry of Transport and Logistics, presented at the first national maritime assises in Tangier on 21 May. The plan proposes 21 new vessels by 2030, about 3.4 billion DH of investment and more than 1,200 direct and indirect jobs, with a 3.6 billion DH annual turnover. The initiative follows a royal call made on 6 November 2023 and responds to heavy dependence on foreign carriers, which handle over 95% of foreign trade by sea.
items.impact: For forwarders and agents, a Moroccan-flagged fleet could in time shift part of the Europe-Morocco RoRo, RoPax, dry bulk and feeder volumes to local operators, changing carrier options and pricing. The proposals on tonnage tax, leasing and simpler port procedures are still recommendations, so near-term operations are unlikely to change.
items.action: Monitor the government's response to the roadmap and any legislation on tonnage tax, leasing and cabotage rules for national operators; no immediate action is required.

items.title: Morocco's Nador West Med and Dakhla gain weight as Atlantic route traffic grows
items.originalTitle: Najib Cherfaoui : «Le Maroc est une puissance maritime internationale»
items.summary: Expert Najib Cherfaoui argues that Morocco's ports, including Tanger Med, Nador West Med and the planned Dakhla Atlantique, are becoming strategically important on world shipping routes. He cites the SECA sulphur rules in force from May 2025, which he says shift some Mediterranean traffic towards the West African route, and the return of ships to the Gibraltar to Cape of Good Hope routing. He also calls for port concession contracts to include clauses on bunker surcharges and Moroccan shipping development.
items.impact: For forwarders and shipping agents, the shift towards the Atlantic route could change service options, transit patterns and port calls for Moroccan cargo. Bunker costs are rising under the SECA rules, with the expert citing a surcharge of around 200 dollars per tonne. Proposed concession clauses on fuel and freight surcharges have not been adopted and are only described as intentions.
items.action: Monitor carrier announcements on new services and routings via Nador West Med and Dakhla Atlantique, and track any concession terms on surcharges that could affect Moroccan import and export costs.

items.title: Spanish international ro-ro short-sea traffic fell 1% in 2025, led by Atlantic declines
items.originalTitle: Debilidad de los tráficos ro-ro exteriores
items.summary: Short-sea shipping in Spain fell 4.3% in 2025 to 257.5 million tonnes, with international traffic down 6.4%. International ro-ro volumes slipped 1% to 28.4 million tonnes, as loadings dropped 2.4% while discharges rose 0.7%. Atlantic ro-ro traffic fell 8.7%, while the Mediterranean rose 0.6%, and Algeciras–Tanger Med truck movements show weakness in early 2026.
items.impact: Forwarders using Spanish ro-ro services should expect a softer market on Atlantic routes, where Santander and Vigo saw sharp falls, while Mediterranean links to Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia grew. On the Strait, truck volumes on Algeciras–Tanger Med were 0.69% lower in the first five months of 2026, and passenger vehicle traffic on the Tanger Med line rose 4.62%.
items.action: Monitor Algeciras–Tanger Med truck capacity and pricing for signs of further weakness, and review Atlantic ro-ro bookings out of Santander and Vigo given the steep declines.

items.title: Valenciaport container traffic holds steady as rail and vehicle volumes climb
items.originalTitle: Valenciaport container traffic holds steady as vehicle traffic rises
items.summary: Container traffic at terminals managed by the Port Authority of València is virtually stable, with the rolling twelve-month total at 5,628,895 TEUs, up 0.15%. Rail traffic reached 258,910 TEUs, up 20.26% on 2025, and vehicle traffic handled as cargo rose 9%.
items.impact: Stable container volumes at Valencia mean no new capacity pressure is signalled for forwarders routing through the port. The strong growth in rail traffic points to more inland rail options linked to Valenciaport, which may suit forwarders moving cargo onward by rail. The rise in ro-ro vehicle cargo may affect space and scheduling for vehicle shippers.
items.action: Monitor rail service availability and terminal capacity at Valencia if your inland or onward moves depend on rail; no immediate action is required on the summary figures alone.

items.title: Rotterdam biofuel bunker premiums widen as conventional VLSFO prices fall sharply
items.originalTitle: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: B30 premiums widen as conventional bunker prices drop
items.summary: Rotterdam's B30-VLSFO premium over conventional VLSFO widened by $55/mt to $194/mt as the conventional price dropped $48/mt to $678/mt. Singapore and Hong Kong biofuel blend premiums also widened, while Singapore's bio-blended bunker sales fell 33% in October to 54,000 mt. Dutch ZRE-A ticket prices fell from €197.5 to €170/mtCO2e over the week.
items.impact: Biofuel blends are becoming more expensive relative to conventional fuel in Rotterdam, Singapore and Hong Kong, so the cost gap for ships choosing B30 has widened. Antwerp's B100 price sits about $666/mt above Rotterdam because Belgium has no RED III mechanism, which raises the cost of bio-blended fuel bunkered there. Lower ZRE-A ticket prices may also have reduced support for Rotterdam's biofuel prices.
items.action: Forwarders and agents with clients on biofuel bunker contracts should compare the blend premium against conventional VLSFO before fixing supply, and monitor Rotterdam ZRE-A ticket prices and feedstock barge prices for further movement.

items.title: EU and Indonesia sign trade agreement removing duties on most goods
items.originalTitle: 90% des exportations indonésiennes vers l'UE seront exonérées de droits de douane: Bruxelles officialise un vaste accord commercial avec Jakarta (notamment pour du textile et de l'huile de palme)
items.summary: The European Union and Indonesia formally signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) and an investment protection agreement in Brussels on 21 November. The deal removes customs duties on more than 98% of EU exports to Indonesia, and Indonesia says about 90% of its exports to the EU will be duty-free, including palm oil, footwear, textiles and seafood. It still needs European Parliament approval and Indonesian ratification before provisional entry into force, which is expected in early 2027.
items.impact: EU food, agricultural and industrial exporters should see lower duty costs on Indonesian-bound cargo, and importers of Indonesian textiles, palm oil, footwear and seafood should see lower duties on entry to the EU. Savings are estimated at over 600 million euros a year, but the benefits will only apply after entry into force, so current shipments remain subject to existing tariffs. Palm oil and deforestation were key sticking points, and a dedicated palm oil protocol and sustainability cooperation mechanisms are included.
items.action: No change to current procedures yet. Monitor the European Parliament vote and Indonesia's ratification timetable, and prepare origin documentation and supplier certification for preferential claims ahead of entry into force.

items.title: Long Beach and Los Angeles mark 20 years of clean air plan
items.originalTitle: San Pedro Bay Ports Mark 20 Years of Landmark Clean Air Action Plan
items.summary: The ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles marked 20 years since adopting the Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP), which has cut port-related diesel particulate matter by 90%, nitrogen oxides by 70% and sulfur oxides by 98% since 2005. The next phase focuses on moving zero-emission cargo-handling equipment and drayage trucks from demonstration to broader deployment, backed by a Cooperative Agreement with the South Coast Air Quality Management District and new CAAP Plus incentives. The ports are also pursuing cleaner marine fuels and Green Shipping Corridors with Asian ports.
items.impact: For forwarders and shipping agents using San Pedro Bay, the push towards zero-emission trucks and cargo-handling equipment may bring future changes to terminal equipment, charging and fuelling arrangements, and possibly truck access requirements. The article gives no specific new charges, deadlines or rules for cargo owners at this stage. Costs of the transition are acknowledged but not quantified.
items.action: No immediate action is required. Monitor the zero-emission infrastructure plans that both ports are developing with terminal and utility partners, with initial drafts expected next May, and check with your Long Beach and Los Angeles terminal operators for any equipment or access changes.

items.title: Dry bulk freight rates mixed as Atlantic firms and Pacific softens

items.summary: Dry bulk rates were mixed in the week to 23 November 2026. Panamax and Kamsarmax rates were supported in the Atlantic by limited prompt tonnage and healthy mineral enquiry, while Pacific rates came under pressure from slowing Australian mineral demand and growing tonnage availability. Ultramax and Handysize markets were broadly steady, with firmer pockets in the Atlantic and US Gulf.

Period rates and scrubber benefits to charterers are also relevant to longer-term cost planning.
items.action: Monitor weekly Atlantic and Pacific fixture levels before committing to new bulk freight, particularly for early December laycans. No immediate action is required for container or general cargo.

items.title: Hormuz traffic stays 65% below pre-war levels as six tankers attacked
items.originalTitle: Strait Of Hormuz Traffic Stays 65% Below Pre-War Levels As 6 Tankers Are Attacked In A Week
items.summary: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz stayed about 65% below pre-conflict levels in mid-November, with 263 transits in the seven days to 18 November, down from 308 the week before. UKMTO reported attacks on six tankers in the week, including two in the Persian Gulf, and one crew member was reported missing on each of two affected vessels. The JMIC rates the threat level in the strait as severe.
items.impact: Reduced transit capacity through the strait raises the risk of delays and cost pressure on Gulf-linked cargo, particularly energy and LPG. Attacks near Khasab and the strait itself make war-risk cover, crew safety and routing decisions central to planning. UKMTO cannot verify all US-facilitated transits, so official counts may understate the true incident picture.
items.action: Check with carriers and war-risk insurers on routing, surcharges and sailing reliability for Gulf calls, and watch UKMTO and JMIC updates before committing to Hormuz transits.

Container rates from Asia to the US were mostly lower, with Drewry reporting falls of 5% to Los Angeles and 9% to New York, while US Gulf chemical tanker rates were mostly higher on the USG-to-ARA and USG-to-Brazil lanes.
items.impact: A strike could halt operations at eight terminals and affect vessel, yard and gate activity, with a significant rail backlog already slowing inland moves of holiday inventory. Analysts expect limited effect on Black Friday goods, but other holiday cargo still in port could face delays and some deliveries may be threatened.
items.action: Importers and forwarders shipping into LA/LB should check cargo status, prepare contingency routings and monitor the contract outcome after the Saturday expiry.

items.title: UK carbon border charge hits Moroccan fertiliser imports from January 2027
items.originalTitle: Le Royaume-Uni soumet les engrais marocains à une vérification carbone propre à son mécanisme frontal
items.summary: HMRC has set out how UK importers can declare the actual emissions of goods under the UK carbon border adjustment mechanism, which starts on 1 January 2027 and covers aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel. Importers can use verified actual emissions or HMRC default values, and the verifier must hold a process-specific accreditation to ISO/IEC 17029 and ISO 14065. The charge applies the sectoral quarterly rate to embedded emissions, less any carbon price already paid in the country of production.
items.impact: Moroccan fertiliser exports to the UK will carry a carbon cost from 2027, unless the importer declares actual emissions verified by an accredited third party. Default values are binding once chosen and cannot be corrected later, and they are set high for ammonia and nitric acid, so the default route may be costly for some producers. Registration is needed for importers buying at least £50,000 of covered goods in a 30-day window or having passed that amount in the previous twelve months, with the first declaration and payment due by 31 May 2028.
items.action: Moroccan producers and their UK clients should decide now whether to use actual or default emissions, and start monitoring emissions over the full calendar year 2027 with an accredited verifier. Producers should prepare to pass CN code, net weight, verified emissions intensity, intermediate material data and any carbon taxes paid in Morocco to UK customers.

items.impact: Moroccan exporters could sell to China without paying Chinese import duties, which may improve margins and competitiveness on eligible products. Forwarders and exporters will need proof of origin that meets the Chinese rules, so documentation through ADII will be central to claiming the benefit. The article gives no effective date, product list or start date for the measure, so the scope remains unclear.
items.action: Exporters and forwarders should obtain the Chinese rules of origin annexed to the ministry notice and check which HS codes are covered. Confirm the certificate of origin procedure with ADII before shipping, and watch for the effective date and product scope.

items.summary: The UK and EU struck a food trade deal at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels, which the government says will remove costly paperwork and border checks for food and plants. The government estimates the deal could add up to £5.1bn to the UK economy in the long term.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers moving food and plants between the UK and EU should expect fewer certificates, less documentation and fewer border checks once the deal takes effect, which could cut costs per consignment and speed up transit. The article gives no start date, and retailers say the detail is still to be worked through, including regulatory alignment. Until then, existing SPS requirements still apply.
items.action: Monitor for the implementation date and the detailed SPS text, and identify which of your food and plant lines would benefit. Do not change certification or border procedures until the rules are confirmed in force.

Contracts taking effect before that date stay under the MFR until their terms end.

Only one fuel recovery mechanism applies to each contract at a time, so contract start dates will determine which surcharge applies. Quarterly adjustments continue under both mechanisms during the transition.
items.action: Check the start dates of upcoming contracts and quotes against the 1 January 2027 cut-off, and review how fuel surcharges are costed in 2027 pricing. Watch for the Q1 2027 MFS values published on Hapag-Lloyd's tariff page on 1 December 2026.

items.title: IMO Net-Zero Framework faces compromise talks at December MEPC meeting
items.originalTitle: The Week in Alt Fuels: The net-zero bargain
items.summary: The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee meets from 30 November to 3 December to consider proposals ranging from stronger economic measures to removing greenhouse gas pricing altogether. The EU and Pacific Island states back the text approved in April 2025, while the US and several other countries, including major oil producers, want substantial changes to its technical and economic provisions. Shipping associations and some EU member states are pressing for a more flexible, achievable framework that avoids overlapping regional and global charges.
items.impact: A softer Net-Zero Framework could lower future carbon-related costs on ocean freight but could also make compliance cheaper than switching fuels, which may slow investment in cleaner fuels. Forwarders and importers should expect uncertainty over carbon pricing and surcharges until the outcome is clear. Any global deal that replaces overlapping regional charges, such as the EU's own measures, could change how carbon costs are levied on shipments.
items.action: Monitor the outcome of the IMO intersessional GHG working group (23 to 27 November) and the MEPC session (30 November to 3 December). Review contract clauses on bunker and carbon-related surcharges so you can adjust quickly once the framework is settled.

items.impact: The deal lowers the immediate risk of a labour disruption at the largest US container port complex, where a walkout could have affected cargo owners across the supply chain. Watchmen control terminal-gate access at six container terminals, so there were concerns that other union workers might honour their picket lines. Until ratification is confirmed, the risk is reduced rather than removed.
items.action: Keep monitoring for Local 26 ratification results and any published terms, and avoid treating the risk as closed until members vote. Check with carriers and terminals on any changes to gate or cargo handling arrangements at Los Angeles and Long Beach.

items.title: Spain bans scrubber wastewater discharge in all its ports from July 2027
items.originalTitle: Spain to ban all scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports
items.summary: Spain's Council of Ministers approved a royal decree banning ships fitted with any type of scrubber, whatever their flag, from discharging scrubber wastewater in its ports and anchorages from 1 July 2027. The ban covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid systems and replaces local restrictions at several Spanish ports, including Algeciras, Valencia and Barcelona. It aligns with the OSPAR Commission decision but goes further by bringing forward the closed-loop and hybrid ban and extending it beyond OSPAR areas.
items.impact: Ships with scrubbers will not be able to discharge washwater in Spanish ports and anchorages, so they must burn low-sulphur fuel in the regulated areas or hold wastewater on board for handover in port. This may add fuel costs and port-side handling for vessels calling Algeciras, Valencia, Barcelona and other Spanish ports. The uniform national rule should give operators more legal certainty than the current patchwork of local restrictions.
items.action: Vessel operators and agents calling Spanish ports should check which scrubber mode their ships use and plan low-sulphur fuel or wastewater handover arrangements before 1 July 2027. Monitor the royal decree text for detailed compliance requirements.

Forwarders must classify consignments carefully, since the line between waste for recycling and a secondary raw material is now a customs and environmental compliance question decided by authorities. Imports of polymers and recycled granules outside the waste category are not affected.
items.action: Review any consignments of plastic scrap or recyclable plastics from the EU to Morocco and confirm their waste classification with customs before shipping. items.impact: If adopted, the framework would add a carbon price to global shipping, which would feed into freight costs and surcharges on international routes. Delay or a weakened text could lead to regional and national rules, such as those already emerging in Africa and Europe, creating a regulatory patchwork for shippers and carriers. Investment decisions on fuels and fleet electrification are likely to hinge on the outcome.
items.action: Monitor the outcome of the ISWG-GHG-23 talks and MEPC 85 closely, and review exposure to carbon-linked surcharges on your main trade lanes before the decision on 4 December.

items.summary: The European Commission has kept Tanger Med on its list of non-EU transhipment ports, where a container ship call does not break the voyage calculation for EU climate obligations. The obligations fall on carriers rather than Moroccan terminals, but the cost of surrendering allowances under the EU ETS and of FuelEU Maritime compliance may feed into surcharges and routing decisions. Ships calling at intermediate ports with transhipment shares above 65% within 300 nautical miles of an EU port are now treated the same way.
items.action: Forwarders and agents using Tanger Med transhipment should ask carriers how the 10 December change affects their EU voyage calculations and any related surcharges. Monitor the list review, which must take place at least every two years.

items.title: IMO Net-Zero Framework stalls again as fund rules remain unwritten ahead of London talks
items.originalTitle: Analysis: IMO Net-Zero: now-or-never time draws near
items.summary: The IMO Net-Zero Framework was adjourned by a year in October 2025 after US threats, and the draft still does not say who holds the proposed fund or how its money is distributed. ISWG-GHG 23 opens in London on Monday, with the working group meeting 23 to 27 November and MEPC 85 following from 30 November. The article argues that the fund's proceeds, the reward method and a post-2030 price path must be settled before any vote.
items.impact: If adopted, the framework would add a global levy on top of the EU ETS and FuelEU, and carriers would have no vote over the fund. The US opposes it and has threatened visa penalties, port fees and sanctions, so adoption remains uncertain. Existing EU carbon costs continue regardless of the IMO outcome.
items.action: Watch the outcome of ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85 for written fund rules, the reward method and the post-2030 price path. Check freight contracts for how ETS and FuelEU costs are passed through to shippers.

items.title: Mediterranean spot rates rise 6.8% as Red Sea container return stalls
items.originalTitle: Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update: Mediterranean spot rates move in mysterious ways as Red Sea return stalls
items.summary: Far East to Mediterranean spot rates rose 6.8% in the past week to USD 4,989 per FEU on 19 November 2026, while rates on other Far East fronthaul routes continued to soften. Xeneta links the divergence to a November slowdown in container ship transits through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which fell 28% from a peak of 16.6 per day on 25 October to 11.9 on 19 November.
items.impact: Mediterranean-bound cargo from the Far East now costs USD 1,551 per FEU more than North Europe-bound cargo, so budgets for Mediterranean lanes need adjusting. Far East to Mediterranean trades are the most exposed to Red Sea disruption, which can cause sudden rate spikes. Xeneta expects rates to trend downwards into 2027, but not smoothly.
items.action: Monitor Bab el-Mandeb transit counts and Mediterranean spot rates over the coming weeks, and build flexibility and rate contingency into bookings for Far East to Mediterranean cargo.

items.title: Transpacific container spot rates fall while Asia-Med rates unexpectedly spike
items.originalTitle: Transpac spots finally on the slide, but Asia-Med spike a surprise
items.summary: Container spot rates on the transpacific fell for a seventh consecutive week, with Shanghai-New York down 9% to $8,194 per 40ft and Shanghai-Los Angeles down 5% to $7,026. Asia-Mediterranean rates rose instead: Shanghai-Genoa was up 6% to $4,436 per 40ft after three weeks of flat rates, while Shanghai-Rotterdam was unchanged at $3,496. European forwarders said the Asia-Med rise did not match demand or space conditions.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers may see transpacific costs ease in early December, although the US west coast forwarder Freight Right expects rates to stay largely stable and carriers to hold baseline pricing ahead of January. Asia-Med shippers face notified increases of new FAK levels and pre-Chinese New Year peak season surcharges of $1,000 to $1,600 per 40ft, but forwarders doubt these will fully stick. New capacity arriving on the transpacific over the next two to three weeks, including Zim's ZX3 and MSC's Mustang service, adds further downward pressure.
items.action: Watch whether the first-half December Asia-Med increases and the peak season surcharges hold, and look for vessel-specific transpacific promotional rates in early December before committing to bookings.

items.title: Shippers criticise carriers' peak season surcharges and capacity limits amid weak oversight
items.originalTitle: Container shipping rate tactics draw competition criticism
items.summary: Shippers complain about a lack of regulatory oversight in container shipping, as carriers seek to raise earnings through peak season surcharges while restricting capacity. The publisher's summary gives no further detail on specific carriers, routes or amounts.
items.impact: Forwarders and importers may face higher peak season surcharges and tighter space availability on container services. Without clear regulatory oversight, shippers have limited recourse against surcharge levels.

items.title: Drewry World Container Index falls 3% to $4,176 as Transpacific rates keep dropping
items.originalTitle: Drewry: World Container Index Down 3% Last Week
items.summary: The Drewry World Container Index fell 3% to $4,176 per 40ft container in the week to 19 November 2026, driven by lower Transpacific rates, though it remains 126% higher year on year. Shanghai to New York rates dropped 9% to $8,194 and Shanghai to Los Angeles fell 5% to $7,026, both continuing a seven-week downward trend. On Asia-Europe/Med, Shanghai to Genoa rose 6% to $4,436 while Shanghai to Rotterdam held at $3,496.
items.impact: Transpacific shippers should see continued rate softening as carriers cut capacity through blank sailings, with ten announced for next week. Asia-Europe costs are likely to rise in December as carriers push peak season surcharges of $1,000 to $1,600 per 40ft ahead of the new contract season. North Europe port congestion is delaying empty container returns to Asia, raising risk of equipment shortages.
items.action: Monitor Transpacific rates, which Drewry expects to fall further next week, and consider timing bookings accordingly. For Asia-Europe, budget for the proposed PSS surcharges effective December and watch for equipment availability given the North Europe congestion.

items.title: EU and UK conclude talks to link their emissions trading systems
items.originalTitle: EU and UK agree to link Emission Trading Systems (ETS)
items.summary: The EU and UK have concluded negotiations to link their Emissions Trading Systems, announced at the EU-UK summit on 20 November. The linking agreement is committed to apply from 2028, subject to ratification and entry into force in both jurisdictions. It paves the way for a possible mutual exemption from each side's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
items.impact: Once the linking agreement is in force, UK-origin goods would be exempt from the EU CBAM after the EU amends Annex III through a delegated act, and a corresponding UK approach is expected. This would remove double carbon charges and reduce paperwork and costs for businesses trading across the Channel. The exemption is not yet in place and depends on ratification and legal steps in both jurisdictions.
items.action: Monitor ratification progress and the Commission's delegated act amending Annex III, and keep current CBAM declaration processes for UK-origin goods until any exemption takes effect.

items.title: UK-EU carbon market link to extend UK ETS to international shipping from 2028
items.originalTitle: UK-EU carbon market link brings international shipping into UK ETS
items.summary: The linkage of the UK and EU carbon markets will extend the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to international shipping from 2028. The publisher's summary also notes a separate FuelEU-style regime that may create further obligations, though the article text is truncated.
items.impact: Shipping lines and agents calling at UK ports would face carbon costs on international voyages from 2028, which may feed into surcharges and freight pricing. A parallel FuelEU-style regime could add separate fuel-intensity compliance requirements. Forwarders should expect cost pass-through once the rules take effect.
items.action: Monitor the detailed UK-EU linkage text and carrier surcharge announcements, and ask carriers how they plan to handle UK ETS and FuelEU-style costs on 2028 sailings.

items.title: UK Chamber of Shipping urges UK-EU reset to cut ETS and trade costs
items.originalTitle: UK-EU reset must reduce costs for trade and shipping
items.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping is asking the UK and EU to use reset talks on 20 November to reduce trade barriers, cut regulatory costs and support shipping's net zero transition. It urges closer alignment on ETS monitoring, reporting and verification, and wants ETS revenues returned to shipping's decarbonisation. It also calls for protection of ferry, short-sea and lifeline services and progress towards a UK-EU SPS agreement.
items.impact: These are recommendations from industry rather than adopted rules, so no immediate change to costs, paperwork or transit times is confirmed. If the UK extends its ETS internationally or the two sides align emissions monitoring, costs could flow through to UK imports, exports and consumers. Ferry and short-sea operators could also face changes to derogations and border controls.
items.action: No action is needed yet. Monitor the outcome of the reset talks, any UK ETS expansion proposals and changes to SPS or border control arrangements affecting Northern Ireland and ferry routes.

items.title: Moroccan port traffic rises 3.1% to 202.7 million tonnes by end September
items.originalTitle: Maroc: le trafic portuaire augmente de 3,1% à fin septembre 2026
items.summary: Morocco's ports handled 202.7 million tonnes of commercial traffic to the end of September, up 3.1% on the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Equipment and Water. Transhipment grew 7.4% to 105.2 million tonnes and now accounts for 51.9% of total traffic, while domestic traffic fell 1.3% and exports fell 2.4%. Container volumes rose 2.5% to 9.6 million TEU, and phosphate traffic dropped 15.7%.
items.impact: Growth is driven by transhipment, so Moroccan ports are increasingly serving vessels passing through the Strait of Gibraltar rather than cargo for the domestic market. Forwarders may see continued strength in container capacity, but exporters and phosphate shippers face weaker volumes. Cabotage and bunkering declines suggest reduced domestic coastal and fuel activity.
items.action: Monitor berth congestion and container availability at Tanger Med and other Moroccan hubs as transhipment volumes keep rising, and check phosphate and cereal shipment plans against the reported declines.

items.title: EU Customs Authority holds first management board meeting in Lille, elects chairperson
items.originalTitle: EU Customs Authority holds first management board meeting in Lille
items.summary: The European Union Customs Authority (EUCA) held its first management board meeting in Lille, electing Malgorzata Krok of Poland as Chairperson and adopting core governance and administrative procedures. The agency is a key part of the EU Customs Reform, which entered into force in September, and will coordinate national customs administrations and support EU-level risk analysis. Its activities are scheduled to begin as soon as possible in 2027, with full capacity foreseen after 2030.
items.impact: For forwarders and importers, the EUCA will gradually shift customs risk analysis and controls towards common EU priorities, and it will develop the EU Customs Data Hub to replace over 100 national customs systems. Near-term effects on declarations and clearance are unlikely, as the agency only begins operating in 2027 and reaches full capacity after 2030. Longer term, expect more harmonised controls across Member States.
items.action: No immediate action is required. Monitor EUCA setup milestones and EU Customs Data Hub timelines, and plan for changes to national systems as they migrate.

items.title: IMO's MEPC 85 faces divide over Net-Zero Framework adoption
items.originalTitle: MEPC 85 to confront net-zero divide
items.summary: The IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85) meets in London to resolve differences over draft MARPOL Annex VI amendments and mid-term greenhouse gas measures under the 2023 IMO strategy. The Clean Shipping Coalition urges adoption of the Net-Zero Framework 'as is' before the end of the year, while the Union of Greek Shipowners criticises the EU's negotiating stance and calls for a broader, more flexible approach.
items.impact: The outcome could set a global fuel standard and economic mechanism for international shipping, affecting future fuel and operating costs. Continued delay keeps uncertainty over the sector's decarbonisation pathway, making long-term cost planning harder for forwarders, agents and importers.
items.action: No immediate action is required; monitor the MEPC 85 outcome and any decision on adopting the Net-Zero Framework before year end.
